newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn court postpones verdict on Nazis' slaves.
newsitem.headline: Bonn court postpones verdict on Nazis' slaves.

text.p: A Bonn court delayed a verdict on Friday on whether Germany should pay 21 elderly Jewish women compensation for their unpaid work in Hitler's slave labour camps more than 50 years ago.
The court said that before it could agree the claims it had to be sure the claimants had not already won awards under the federal compensation law that covers victims of the Nazis.
"So far the court has assumed the claimants did not receive such awards. But if they did, this will stand in the way of compensation payments," the court said in a statement.

The verdict on the case had been due on January 31 but was posponed for two months to clear the query. The final ruling could pave the way for thousands of compensation claims from former slave labourers.

Baron von Muenchhausen, who represents the women, said the ruling was a "delaying tactic" by the Bonn finance ministry which is handling the lawsuit against the German government. Most of the women live outside Germany.

He told Reuters that now the women would have to say whether they had received earlier compensation. He said this would probably only affect one of the claimants, a German Jew. The others, originally from Poland and Hungary, were not affected.

"This is something that the court should have established right at the beginning of the five-year case. It's a trick to delay the case further," said Muenchhausen, who works at the Raphael Lemkin Institute of Xenophobia and Genocide at Bremen University and has been representing the women for 10 years.
"We remain optimistic about the outcome of the case. It's not a matter of "if' they are going to award compensation but "how much'."
The finance ministry says it will not comment on the case while the trial is in progress.
The Constitutional Court ruled in July that foreign citizens' claims for their unpaid work as slaves could not be rejected out of hand as violating international law.
But it said the claims might be turned down if they were already covered by specific bilateral agreements with their countries of origin.
The court said German citizens were entitled to make claims too.
The case concerns 21 women, all of them Jewish. Most of the women have now taken Israeli citizenship. Two are U.S. citizens and one is Canadian.

Muenchhausen said the women, who worked for German industry during World War Two, were suing the German government because it had failed to keep its laws in order and had allowed their "rightful" compensation get blocked by legal snags.

He said that previous compensation claims had failed because of this. An exception is IG Farben, which produced Zyklon B for the Nazis' gas chambers and paid the Jewish Claims Conference 30 million marks in 1957.
